# Foreword {.unnumbered}

Every multinational now says that geopolitics matters to it. Far fewer can say *how much*, *through
which channel*, or *what they would do differently if the number changed*. The gap is not one of
attention — boards discuss sanctions, export controls, wars and elections every quarter — but of
measurement. Geopolitical risk reaches a firm through its market access, its inputs, its finance,
its people and its data, and each of those channels can be counted. Most firms do not count them.

This book is the lecture notes of a twelve-session graduate course that tries to close that gap. Its
method is simple and a little stubborn: **every big idea is read, then rebuilt from its data.** A
landmark article or book — Caldara and Iacoviello's geopolitical risk index, Baldwin's *Great
Convergence*, Kuziemko and Werker on the price of a Security Council seat, the Global Sanctions Data
Base — is paired with a practice round in which the data are collected at source and its central
figure is replicated in Tableau. A famous chart is a set of decisions: which countries, which years,
which deflator, which coding rule. You only see the decisions when you make them yourself.

::: {.step}
**The data will disagree with the paper.** Sources are revised, codebooks change, countries are
renamed and recoded. Every practice round records at least one place where the replication did not
match — and asks what that disagreement means for a firm that would have relied on the original.
:::

Each chapter ends on the same question: *what does this figure not license a multinational to
conclude?* That is the habit the course is built to leave behind.

## How to use it {.unnumbered}

| If you want to | Go to |
|---|---|
| Prepare for next week | the session's **Before the session** |
| Re-read the argument after class | the session's **The lecture** |
| Know exactly what the practice round asks | the session's **In the practice** |
| Find where something was covered | the **search box**, top of the sidebar |
| Find a dataset, its URL and its traps | [Data sources](data-sources.qmd) |
| Know how you are graded | [Assessment](assessment.qmd) |

::: {.check}
**The search box is the reason this book exists.** Slides are good for a room and bad for finding
something three weeks later. Search covers every session at once, so a term you half-remember —
*weaponised interdependence*, *ideal points*, *Herfindahl* — takes you to the session that introduced
it, with its reading and its exercise.
:::

## The slides {.unnumbered}

Each chapter links to the decks it was built from. The slides remain the version delivered in class;
the book is the same material as continuous prose, which is the better form for reading afterwards.
All decks are also listed on the [course site](https://warint.github.io/geopolitics-geoeconomics/).

## The twelve chapters {.unnumbered}

| | Chapter | Question |
|---|---|---|
| [1](session-01.qmd) | What is geopolitical risk? | Before we can manage geopolitical risk, what exactly are we counting? |
| [2](session-02.qmd) | The international economic order | Who wrote the rules multinationals play by — and what happens to the rules when the writers' share of the world shrinks? |
| [3](session-03.qmd) | Anarchy and the balance of the major powers | In a system with no government above states, who sets the terms of trade — and how would a multinational know that the balance is shifting? |
| [4](session-04.qmd) | Trade, conflict and geoeconomic fragmentation | If states trade more with friends than with rivals, how does a multinational find out which side each of its markets is on — and how fast the lines are hardening? |
| [5](session-05.qmd) | International institutions | When a multinational relies on an international institution to manage its risk, is it relying on a rule — or on the states that buy and sell influence inside it? |
| [6](session-06.qmd) | Private authority, standards and global regulation | Most of the rules that govern a multinational's daily operations were not written by a government. Who wrote them, with whose power — and does trade spread them up or down? |
| [7](session-07.qmd) | Measuring risk: content analysis, coding, big data and composite indices | Every geopolitical risk score a multinational buys or builds is a chain of choices: which texts, which words, which coder, which weights. Can you see the chain — and defend each link? |
| [8](session-08.qmd) | Cyber geopolitics and digital threats | Is cyberspace a new battlefield for great powers — or a new way for old rivals to hurt each other, with multinationals as collateral? |
| [9](session-09.qmd) | The redefinition of economic diplomacy | When states compete for markets, investment and technology, is the multinational the object of diplomacy, its instrument — or a diplomat in its own right? |
| [10](session-10.qmd) | Economic sanctions | Sanctions have become the instrument of first resort. Are they an efficient mechanism for regulating geopolitical risk — or a source of it? |
| [11](session-11.qmd) | Space geopolitics | Satellites now carry the position, timing, connectivity and imagery a multinational runs on. When orbit is crowded, contested and dominated by one operator, who holds the risk — and what can the firm do about it? |
| [12](session-12.qmd) | Team presentations | Can you make a board act on your assessment — and say what would change your mind? |
